utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Witness 38, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony yesterday. And I'll now give an opportunity to Mr. Emmerson to continue his cross-examination. Are you ready, Mr. Emmerson, to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Witness 38, yesterday afternoon I was asked to clarify two issues with you. The first concerns previous statement you made, and the second concerns the precise date of the incidents you're describing. I'm going to come back to the date a little later on in my questions, but may I start by clarifying with you the statements that you had made, and again I will put these to you and ask you to confirm, yes or no, that these statements were made at various times. First of all, when you say you had escaped from the KLA and made your way across country to VJ units that you encountered in Batusa, you spoke orally to soldiers of the Yugoslav Army and told them what had happened to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You then, I think, made a video interview with soldiers of the Yugoslav Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And when was that in relation to you coming into contact with the soldiers in Batusa? How long after you first met them did you make the video interview?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there in the tents of the Yugoslav Army for about two hours

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And it was during that time that you made the video, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was after we went in the convoy with the Yugoslav Army to the village of Molica.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was it on the same day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And after that, I think you were taken by the soldiers to the MUP, where you made a written statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you confirmed for us yesterday that in none of those statements did you mention Ramush Haradinaj because at that time you had no idea that the man you had seen was Ramush Haradinaj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You then told us that you did not make any further statement about these events at any time before you left Kosovo in June 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And we have looked next at the statement that you made to the MUP in December 2005 [sic]; we looked at that yesterday afternoon. And I think you can confirm that you did not, during that interview, mention a jeep, someone speaking the word "commander," or tell the officers that you had recognised Ramush Haradinaj from the television, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, later, much later, you made a statement to an investigator from the ICTY Prosecution whose name was Roel. Do you remember making that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, just a matter that -- a very, very minor matter. The date of the MUP statement, December 2005, as it appears in the transcript, I think that's just a minor mistake. That's all. It should be fixed up for the transcript, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, that should read December 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just to be absolutely clear, the MUP statement is December 2002. The statement that you made to the investigator from the ICTY, Witness 38, was made in December 2005; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Had you made any other written statements between the MUP statement in December 2002 and the statement that you made to the OTP investigator in December 2005?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you this: Is it right that the first time you mentioned to anyone in authority the fact that you had recognised Ramush Haradinaj as the fourth man was when you made the statement to the investigator from the ICTY? That was the first time you made that connection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Pardon? What do you mean by "the fourth man"?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I'm not sure if this question is clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Okay. Let me put the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The first time that you mentioned to anyone in authority that you believed you had seen Ramush Haradinaj at the mill where you say you were stripped naked and beaten was in the statement that you made to the ICTY investigator in December 2005, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So that was three years after your MUP statement, seven and a half years after the event, and seven years since you say you had recognised him on the television; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It was also seven months after he had been indicted in these proceedings and the indictment had been made public. Can I ask you, did you know that he had been indicted in these proceedings when you first mentioned to anyone in authority that Ramush Haradinaj was the man you believed you'd seen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we go into closed for just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want to just clarify one or two matters about where you say your family were at the time that you were assaulted and stripped naked. Just follow me, if you will, for a moment. When you were assaulted and stripped naked and tied up before the jeep arrived, were you and your father inside a building or outside the building, the mill?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were outside the mill, by the mill, and the rest of the family members were some 5 or 7 metres away from us in the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So they were also outside the mill throughout this, were they, throughout this beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And similarly, during the assault that you say took place after the jeep had left, were you and your father outside or inside the mill?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were outside the mill throughout all that time. We were never inside the mill.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the rest of your family, were they also outside the mill during the second assault that took place after the jeep had left? Were your family also outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were outside the mill.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So your family -- neither you nor your family went inside the mill at all between the start of the assault and the end of the second assault? Between the start of the first assault and the end of the second assault, neither you nor your family went inside the mill building, or any other building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. We never went inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, you told us yesterday that at one point either your sister or your sister-in-law took some children a little way away so that the children would not see what was happening to you. When they were taken a little way away, were they still, then, outside the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, outside the building. They were just taken a bit away from us so as not to see the torture that was being accorded us.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you are absolutely clear, are you, that you had been stripped and beaten and tied up before the jeep arrived? There's no doubt about that in your mind at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No doubt at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could we please look on the screen at Defence doc. identification 1D1421, please. 1D1421. Just to remind the court officer, all of these exhibits are not to be published.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, that would be number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be Exhibit number D2, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, Witness 38, you've told us that you don't speak English. I take it you don't read English either.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So I'm going to read to you slowly the passages I want to draw your attention to, to let the interpreters translate them for you, all right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, you had two meetings before you came to give your evidence with the lawyers for the Prosecution who you can see to your right; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: At the first meeting, Mr. Re, the gentleman with the silver hair immediately to your right, was present with Mr. Di Fazio, who we see as the next counsel along in the line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You then had a second meeting on Tuesday of this week in which Mr. Di Fazio was there but Mr. Re was not. Do you remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we please look on the screen at page 5 of this document. And if we could just -- yes, thank you very much. If we could just move the screen -- move the text up a little bit so that the words "Proofing continued at the 6th of March" are at the top of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, I want to just read to you and, where appropriate, summarise to you what you are recorded as having told Mr. Di Fazio. First of all, you are recorded as saying, and I'll just read you the words: "The place in the Gaciferi house where we were kept was a garage in the Gaciferi compound. Present in the garage were myself," and then you list a number of members of your family. You go on to say: "A KLA member came and he said my family should follow him. I really can't remember if the" is it "Djulija family came with us to the mill or not. I remember seeing them later." You then confirmed that you went to a mill about 200 metres away in the middle of the woods, and it was a water mill. You then said: "Half an hour later Aslan Luluni came and a boy from the Tofa family (Nimon's nephew) came. The young guy was dressed in civilian clothes. We were grouped sitting on the ground in the rain. I remember the Suzuki, and I think it belonged to Muharem Knushi (Giqa). That's when the man I know as Haradinaj turned up. He came with him. There had been no mistreatment at this stage. Giqa and the person I think was Ramush Haradinaj were talking. They had a walkie-talkie. They stood away from us. Giqa had a black uniform." And then you describe what Mr. Haradinaj, you say, was wearing. You say: "They did not mention the name Ramush Haradinaj but they did use the word 'commander'" You then say: "The one I think was Ramush said that he had no time and had to go but he did say to Aslan Luluni to keep talking to her." Now, first of all, did the man that you say was Ramush Haradinaj tell Aslan Luluni to keep talking to you or not? Because that's not what you told us yesterday.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed because he returned immediately that he was in some place of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So that was something that you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he got orders to continue talking to me, in fact. That's what I assumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That was something you assumed; it wasn't something that you heard said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear him say anything. I just heard the word "commander," that he immediately returned and start -- the same thing started all over again. He started beating us and ill-treating us all over again.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Why did you tell Mr. Di Fazio --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I object to that question. These aren't -- the witness hasn't adopted these. This is not a statement; these are my notes. The witness has not had them read back to her. She has not had an opportunity to digest them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: She has not had an opportunity to correct them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see Mr. Emmerson accepts that the proper foundation should be laid for it, and if that's not possible, then we might have a different problem. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I don't want to interrupt Mr. Emmerson's examination, but I should remind the Chamber that some time ago I specifically asked that proofing notes be delivered to us in verbatim form so that we would not have this particular problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And we'll raise it again at a later point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's on the record, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, the record of this meeting, Witness 38, says, and I'll ask you in a moment to comment on whether you said these words, but the record made by Mr. Di Fazio says that "At the time the jeep turned up, there had been no mistreatment at this stage." Did you say that to Mr. Di Fazio or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that but a lot of time had passed. But I know that before the jeep came, Aslan was maltreating us and that after the jeep, the same thing continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you said that to Mr. Di Fazio, did you? You made that clear to Mr. Di Fazio while you were having your proofing session, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand your question. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson is asking you the following: He read what has been put on paper of your meeting with Mr. Di Fazio, and he read to you that it says -- and now I read that: "There had been no mistreatment at this stage. Giqa and the person I think was Ramush Haradinaj were talking. They had a walkie-talkie. They stood away from us." Mr. Emmerson would like to know whether that is what you told Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- maybe I was confused. I had some sort of stage fright at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is not what may have explained why you said so, but the first question is: Is what I just read, that is, "There had been no mistreatment at this stage," did you say a similar thing or did you say this, exactly in these words, to Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know. I honestly can't remember. I told him how we were mistreated. But when I told my story, it wasn't in chronology. I skipped from one thing to another. And there was the statement that I gave in Belgrade. But one thing I'm certain of is that I was mistreated before and after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see. Mr. Emmerson, I'd like to -- Could you take your earphones off for a second, please? Mr. Emmerson, and I'm also addressing you, Mr. Re, I am not a native English speaker. When I read: "There had been no mistreatment at this stage," I could -- but please correct me if I'm wrong, this language seems to be, to me at least as a non-English speaker, ambiguous to the extent that it could mean there had been no mistreatment up to and including this stage, or that it could also mean that -- I don't know who drafted it, whether that's a native speaker or not. But literally translated to my language, it could also mean there had been no mistreatment at this stage, so limited to that period of time, until that stage. I don't know--

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: As a matter of English, it can't have that second connotation because the words "had been" refer to everything up to and including that stage. "There had been no mistreatment" means there was no mistreatment prior to that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you at least for that explanation, because it's a subtlety perhaps in the language you have now explained. A simple question to you, Mr. Di Fazio: Is there any audio recording of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, there is not, if Your Honour please. There is no visual or audio recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that could assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: These are my words, my notes based on what was interpreted to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Often after lengthy passages of hearing the witness -- what the interpreter said to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's a summary of what was translated to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I see you're about to be on your feet. I take it at least you find confirmation of what you said earlier in the present discussion and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know how the Chamber wishes to deal with it, because I know we're in the middle of an examination, but this is going to become, obviously, a point of some critical importance, because the position that we potentially will get into is ultimately having, perhaps, someone like Mr. Di Fazio become a witness with regard to what was said, which is, I think, not a position that any of us want to have because it also raises a series of other issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's deal with that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it at this moment I'll try to seek clarification of the most urgent and most necessary points of the matter. And I'd like to invite the witness to put on her earphones again and give you an opportunity to continue, Mr. Emmerson. Witness 38, don't worry about these procedural matters. It's -- we now continue the examination. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Witness 38, did you or did you not tell Mr. Di Fazio on Tuesday that the jeep -- by the time the jeep arrived, you had already been stripped naked and assaulted? Did you tell him that or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that does potentially raise an issue as far as Mr. Di Fazio's position is concerned. May I continue with the cross-examination and raise that issue at the end of this witness' evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that would be better than to again interrupt. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about the evidence you've been -- you've given us about being left naked after you were stripped naked and how long it was that you were naked, and I want to go through the evidence that you've given just to make sure I've understood what you're saying correctly. Now, you told us yesterday that you and your father were stripped naked at the mill and that you were tied up at the mill; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not my father, except while they were searching him. And I was stripped, indeed. Maybe it was mistranslated or misinterpreted, or they simply didn't understand me. My father was not naked. He just had to strip while he was being searched; then he got to put his clothes back on again and I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not -- I'm not -- I'm not trying to disagree with you or to trip you up. I was asking you simply to confirm that both you and your father were forced to remove your clothes for the first time whilst you were at the mill; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both I and my father. However, after my father was searched, he was told to get dressed and it was not like that with me. I was completely naked.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. So your father was told to get dressed and you remained naked. Now, you told us yesterday that you eventually rejoined the convoy and that you were still naked and your hands were still tied when you rejoined the convoy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Roughly what time did this incident at the mill happen? What time of day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in the afternoon. I don't know what time it was, but it was the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And roughly what was the -- at what time did you join the convoy? How long was it between the assault and you rejoining the convoy naked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two hours, two hours and a half was how long the struggle lasted, and then they told me to join the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, that night you've told us you stopped and spent the night, sleeping overnight, in the woods; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you were guarded all night whilst you were in the woods; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the next day, whilst you were still at the same place in the woods, you said a group of men came and were threatening to rape your sister, but one of the men there said, "Why bother with that one when this one is already naked." Do you remember saying that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So are we to assume that you spent the whole night up to that point naked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And were you naked for the whole of the following day, until the next night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And were you naked for the whole of the following night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, until just before sunrise.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And at that point I think you told us that you were allowed to get dressed because you were complaining that you had a fever because you'd been naked in the rain for two nights and one day and half a day. So from the day that you were first stripped at the mill through the first night and the whole of the next day and most of the following night, you'd been naked and you said that you had a fever and were given your clothes back at that point; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Who gave you your clothes back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who was guarding us.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So he'd carried your clothes with you whilst you walked naked from the mill, had he?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 38, the interpreters could not hear your answer. Would you please repeat your answer to the question whether the person guarding you, as Mr. Emmerson suggested, carried your clothes with you whilst you walked naked from the mill. Could you respond to that question, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said my sister had picked up my things and she was carrying them, but she didn't to dare give them to me to get dressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, Witness 38, if it's true that you were held naked for 36 hours in the rain and the cold and in front of so many people along the way, that that must have been a very humiliating experience for you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Very, very humiliating, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's not something you could be mistaken about, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we please look at Defence document identification 1382 in English and 1376 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The document that you're about to see, Witness 38, is, again, the statement that you made to the MUP in -- at the end of 2002, when you told us they came to visit you and you made a statement that you signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand it's Defence Exhibit 1; is that right? Could we look, please, at page 2, at the bottom in the English, and in the Serbian, if we could look please at, also, page 2 of the text, second half of the page. Now, if we can just go down to the paragraph -- yes -- with the word beginning "Negdje," if we can have that paragraph up, please. Before -- I think that's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, we have the English translation of this document, and in that paragraph, Witness 38, you describe what you say Aslan Luluni did to you at 8.00, and you say that he tied your hands, that he made you take your clothes off, that he made you eat your chequebook, your bankbook and that he abused you and hit you and threatened you. And then towards the bottom of the paragraph, you say: "Aslan went along with this and on leaving said to the guard who was with us all the time, 'Don't let them run away or else I'll kill,'" and then we need to go on to page 3 in the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Do we have page 3 in the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There still seems to be different versions. In my English version, this still is on page --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's at the bottom of page -- It should be the last line of page 2. Yes, and we now need to move on to the top of page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But there's still more than what you're reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's obviously printed out differently from mine. Does your paragraph going on: "Then the two of them and Nimon Tofa's son went hurriedly away. Half an hour later the guard told me to get dressed." Do Your Honours have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, on the bottom of page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And if we can go to the very bottom of the Serbian page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Is that your signature at the bottom, Witness 38?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You see, you've been recorded by the police officers who took this statement as saying that you were told to get dressed after half an hour.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember saying that at all. I was not dressed, I was naked.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You speak the same language, don't you, as the person who was taking that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you signed it on that very page.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I signed it. It's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want now to look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you did not ask if you, Witness, read it before signing it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, I was very poorly. I was sedated. I could barely speak and to tell you frankly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We've already looked at this statement, Witness 38, and we've seen all the names you were able to remember and the precise times that you were able to recall at which these incidents took place. We looked at it yesterday afternoon. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You were able to give a precise time for the period of time when you first saw Muharem Knushi at 6.00 p.m. And you were able to give the time of about 8.00 in the evening for the time that you say you were assaulted by Aslan Luluni.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They helped me because they had the same statement, but really I had had a lot of tranquilisers by then. I don't know what I was saying. They have that statement that I gave the first time and I really don't know, I don't quite recall all that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to another topic, briefly. I said to you I was going to come back to the question of dates on which this event occurred, and I want to just clarify with you, first of all, as I've done before at each stage of the way, the testimony you've already given to make sure that we've all understood it properly, because you told us yesterday - and, again, correct me if I have this wrong - you told us yesterday that sometime around the 6th or 7th of May, from your window you saw a group of vehicles arrive and men distributing weapons. Do you remember saying that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. I remember saying that. I think it was in the middle of May. I don't know the exact date. I'm not sure about the date. It's been a long time ago. I know that I gave a statement to the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, the same day that I escaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going back to the day when you saw the vehicles arrive and the weapons being distributed in the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, just to make -- you asked the witness whether she remembered that she said the 6th or the 7th of May. As a matter of fact, the record says that she said mid-May, the 6th or the 7th, apart from any logic in that. But that's what she said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think if Your Honour looks two lines down, she then explains, having clarified, that it was the 6th or the 7th, that it was early May, not mid-May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But the date is probably less important than the chronology. You remember that date, do you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Which evening?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The evening when the men came with the cars and were distributing weapons. You remember that occasion; yes? Shall I put the question again or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember the event but I'm not really sure about the date.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Mr. Emmerson's microphone is on while the witness is speaking which reduces audibility considerably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I did understand, Witness 38, that Mr. Emmerson is not that much focusing on the date but is focusing on the event when the people came and distributed the weapons. Yes? Please focus on that. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, you told us in your evidence yesterday that it was on that same day that a stone was thrown through your window, that night. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You then told us that it was the following day, the day after the weapons had been distributed, that you saw Qemajl Shalja addressing a number of people in the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But before that, I had gone to the democratic party quarters to complain about that rock thrown into my window.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So the day after the rock was thrown, you went first to the democratic party to complain about the rock, and then after that you heard Qemajl Shalja addressing a crowd; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the man at the democratic party suggested that you might like to spend the night with a neighbour, that night; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to go away from my apartment. He said: "I can't do anything to help you, but just move away."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did he say to you that it's probably just a street gang?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And so that night you did stay with your neighbour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And did your sister-in-law go with you to stay with your neighbour that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: She did.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you say it was in the morning, the following morning, that you heard gun-fire towards the house of your neighbour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard it myself from the house where we were sleeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then you went from that house to your own apartment, avoiding the gun-fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And did you go back to your own house with your sister-in-law?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They joined us a bit later. We couldn't all go in a group. We had to go one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But you were back at your flat by the time your sister-in-law got there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then you said some KLA men came in, or some men came in, I think two in uniform and two in civilian clothes, but it's perhaps not critical at the moment, but some men came into the flat and told you to stick together and join the convoy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The convoy, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And that those men were being nice to you, were they, trying to help you, those particular men at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So just to recap the timing, was it later that same day that you were abused at the mill?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So to be absolutely clear, you were abused at the mill two days after you first saw the men arrive with the weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, before we look at the statement that you made to the Prosecution in this case, I wonder if I can just briefly to ask you one or two questions about what happened whilst you were in the flat, between going from your neighbour's house and leaving to join the convoy. First of all, was there ever an occasion whilst you were in the flat when anybody fired bullets into your flat, so that bullets landed in the -- in your flat whilst you were in there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was strong fire by that time. There was a lot of fighting. My own apartment and my neighbours were targeted. Everybody came out of their houses and apartments, and that's how the convoy was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let me put my question again. Did any bullets land in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have time to look, but there is a bullet-hole in the wall, yes, on the front side.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could we look briefly, please - and it will be brief - at Defence document identification 1463, and in the Albanian, 1469, and at page 3 of that document, paragraph 8. Paragraph 8 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we move on, I'd like to seek one clarification. Witness 38, you said you stayed overnight in the house of a neighbour. You were talking about going from your apartment to the neighbour's house. Now, the neighbour's house, is that also an apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A privately owned house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that's not in the same block as where your apartment was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: These men who came into your apartment to help you out and take you to the convoy, they weren't accusing you of killing anybody, were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, later some --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could other microphones be switched off? Can the witness please repeat? We didn't hear any of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please repeat your answer, but perhaps could the -- yes. Could you please repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They told us to get out of our homes, of our houses, to join the column. They did not mistreat us, and I couldn't recognise them because they were wearing masks. There were masked people, and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But you're absolutely clear that they were trying to help you and were being nice to you at that point.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they just told us to get out, and they just didn't let us put any more clothes on. I had to get out in the track suit I happened to be wearing. I just grabbed my bag with my personal papers that was handy, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So could we please look in the English then at page 3, paragraph 8, and also in the Albanian, at paragraph 8 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I use the words "thank you, Madam Registrar," to confirm that it's a Chamber's decision without spoken communication earlier; I agree with the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I will begin to pick up those formalities as a matter of second nature as the trial proceeds. I'm sorry if from time to time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But just before we look, then, at your witness statement for this chronology, you mentioned yesterday that you initially joined the convict -- the convoy in the centre of Junik, but then you asked to go in the direction of Rastavica but they wouldn't let you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions a little later on about that. Now, could we look, please, at the witness statement you made to the Prosecution in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Which is Defence document identification 1429 in the English, and the Albanian is attached at 1446.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Turn your microphone off, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has that got a number already? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not yet. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number D4, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: First of all, could we just look to the bottom of the page for you to confirm that that was your signature. I think the -- in fact, I think your signature may appear on the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could we just briefly show the witness the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: There are a number of signatures, Mr. Emmerson, aren't there?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The one where you see the witness' name, on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That is your signature, is it, on the left-hand side of that sheet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And just so that we're clear how this statement came to be recorded, you were interviewed, I think, on two days, the 13th and 14th of December, by a Prosecution investigator called Roel Versonnen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And at the end of the interview, a statement was compiled from what you had said and read over to you in Serbian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you were told that you could add anything or change anything that was incorrect about the statement, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, you knew that you were being asked to sign or put your initials on every page, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you knew that the statement was supposed to record the truth, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May we, again, ask a little more complete. Witness, did you also read yourself before what you then signed, or did you think -- did you not read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They read it out to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- I think it's a clear position that this statement was recorded in English and then read out to the witness, who was asked then to sign each page and subsequently translated into Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So if we can just start with the chronology point, first of all, just to make sure we've got our dates correct. If you look at paragraphs 12, 13, and 14, please, if they could be brought up on the screen. The only point I want to direct your attention to is that these paragraphs describe the event where vehicles turn up and weapons are distributed, and I'm just asking you to confirm, in the first line of paragraph 13, that the date you then gave, as best you could, was the 10th of May; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, what I'm going to do is to go through those paragraphs of your statement which take the chronology on. I know that others are very familiar with this document so that if I, in any way, make a mistake, I will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we drop down to paragraph 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 23, you say that on that same evening, when you'd seen the weapons being distributed, a friend of yours who was Albanian came to see you that evening when the weapons had arrived and advised you to take your children out of Junik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was towards the end of April or thereabouts. Yes, she did come, that much is true, but I think that that took place in late April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Emmerson, you see, I'm looking -- following in the e-court system. We're talking about the statement dated -- is that the 21st of January, 2007? Is that the one?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, then I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because I have a statement in front of me which I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think you be looking at the last witness's statement that I put in, in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we be clear, the one that needs to be on the screen now should have, in its English version, a document identification 1429.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got the wrong one in front of me so I'll not bother you with the problems with that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But does Your Honour have the right one now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not yet, but I'll find it. Please proceed. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I ask whether either of Your Honour's colleagues have a similar difficulty?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, it's just my struggle with the e-court system. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So, sir, if we could just look at paragraph 23, you there told the investigator that it was on the same evening, or you're recorded as having told the investigator that it was on the same evening as the guns were distributed that your friend asked you, or suggested to you, that you should take your children out of Junik. Do you see that? It says so in terms: "On the very evening when the weapons had arrived."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that evening, not that evening when the weapons were being distributed. I had sent my children away in April. It is true that she suggested that I should send my children away, but that was not that evening. There was no way my children could have been there that evening or that I could have sent them then that night, sent them away anywhere, to Belgrade or anywhere. Otherwise, everything was blocked at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm not -- I mean, that's exactly what I'm exploring with you, whether you're right about that, Witness 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let's look over to the following page and paragraph 26, please. If we look at paragraphs 26 and then 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You there say, that night, that you took your three children by bus to Belgrade, accompanied by your Albanian friend, that you left your children with relatives in Belgrade and returned to Kosovo by bus with the friend the same day. And if we then look at 29, you say you spent that night in Gjakova and then walked to Junik the following day. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You can see in your witness statement all of that is supposed to have happened after, and immediately after, the weapons were distributed. Now, are you telling us now that it happened before the weapons were distributed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I'm saying. It was before that. Roads had already been blocked and I had -- the only option I had was this last bus that was going to Belgrade from Junik. She helped me out and I heeded her advice. But the weaponry came only later, after I had returned to my apartment. But the children, my children, had already gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And do you think that you made that clear when you were speaking to the OTP investigator and he's written down what you said wrongly, or do you think that you may have said what he has written down and you have signed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there might have been a mistake, perhaps. I did not tell them the exact date. I don't even remember it exactly now. I know that it was in April that I sent my children to Belgrade, although I do think that nobody actually asked me about the exact date when that had happened, and I had taken my children to Belgrade before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, whether they asked you or not, you told them in terms, in paragraph 23, that all of this happened on the night that you saw the weapons being distributed. It says that -- the statement is as clear as it can be, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know that it is written here, but there is no way I could have taken my children to Belgrade that same night, so I say I may have made a mistake. I might have mis-explained myself. But what I do know is that I had sent my children away from home in April, so there is no way I could have sent them -- taken them to Belgrade on another night.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So if we now look at paragraphs 30 and 31, you say that when you got back to Junik after dropping your children off in Belgrade, you saw then that there were armed men all over the village and you say the situation was chaotic and tense and that you did not dare to leave your apartment for two weeks. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So what you told --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What you told the Prosecution investigator was that there was at least two weeks between you seeing the weapons distributed and the war breaking out in Junik. Now, is that right or is it wrong?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I saw on the entrance to Junik, when I was returning on foot with my friend, a manned check-point, manned by KLA -- KLA members who were armed, whereas all the people in the centre of Junik had not been armed yet by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The question I was asking you is whether there was a two-week interval between you seeing the weapons being distributed and the outbreak of war, as you've described it, in Junik; and that during those two weeks you were inside your flat. Is that true or is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From April, and for two weeks after that, I was in the apartment. But when they threw the rock into my window, that is what I saw with my very own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, if we look at paragraph 35, you say that happened on the 27th of May. Is that right or is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that it is on the 27th of May, but I do not remember the date. I may have said the 27th of May, but I do know that I took my children to Belgrade in the month of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the night when the rock was thrown, you say you went the following day to speak to the president of the democratic party and you spent the following night at your neighbour's house; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, good.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So that would mean that the war broke out on the morning of the 29th, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, approximately so, but I cannot really recall the dates now exactly. I cannot recall that. It is true that I went to Ruzdija's place and I asked her to help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, can we now look at what you told the OTP investigator what happened inside the flat when you went back there. Can you look at paragraph 45. I just want to ask you about that. What condition was the flat in when you went back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got back after four months or so, a bit more, my apartment was -- my apartment was a shambles. It was chaos. There was a killed dog in each of the rooms and everything was pock-marked, and all the walls and the pictures in the house, the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That was in June. This passage of your statement is referring to the condition your house was in when you went back that morning from your neighbour's house. If we look at paragraph 44: "We managed to leave the house through the garden. We sneaked back to my apartment. When we arrived at my apartment, I could see that the front door was wide open, the lock was --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "And the lock was broken and our belongings were scattered around. After ten minutes, three armed KLA soldiers came into the apartment." Was the apartment in that condition when you went back there, or was your father and other relatives inside the apartment as you told us yesterday? What was the condition of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in the apartment; my father and my step-mother were sleeping in the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Had it been ransacked? Was the door broken; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I knew that my father was there with his wife and he went to unharness the horse which was in the garden. And I didn't have time to ask him any questions. We just went in and went out and joined the column, and I never asked later about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, I'm not asking about what you said to your father. I'm asking you a simple question. And with respect, Witness 38, you must know the answer to this because you were in the flat and you've told us you were packing your belongings when the KLA men came in, or you packed your belongings once the KLA men came in. Now, you've told us now that your father was there. I'm asking you whether what you said to the OTP investigator, that the house was -- the front door was wide open, the lock was broken, and your belongings were scattered around, is true or not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. It is. That is what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Is it true, what you stated, or not? Was the house in that -- flat in that condition; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The door was wide open when I came from my neighbour's place, and I was unable, in fact, to pack my belongings but just a little bag in which I kept my personal papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, I'm looking at the clock. Could you give us an indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Fifteen minutes at the most. Probably ten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask other counsel, how much time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I had intended on approximately 15 minutes. I believe, based on Mr. Emmerson's examination thus far, that I probably have questions that will not go further than three or four minutes. And to the extent that Mr. Emmerson may need any additional time, if such is the case, I would be happy to cede my time to him and limit myself to three or four minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I will not be any time at all with this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Then I suggest, Mr. Emmerson, let's see whether you can finish within the next ten minutes and then -- we'll then have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we now look to page 63 of this statement where you deal with what took place at the mill, and I'm going to be ask you about paragraphs 63 all the way down to 74. Can we start with 63, first of all, just to set the scene, you say: "We all went outside" -- this is before you got to the mill and you were in Gacifer. "We all went outside, me and my family, and Isuf Djaljiaj and his wife, they took us to an old mill in the woods. They told us to sit on the ground next to the mill and left us there with one KLA soldier from Junik whose name I cannot remember. He was armed with a semi-automatic rifle and dressed in civilian clothes." Now, is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And that was not Aslan Luluni, because you knew his name, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "He told us to keep quiet because the boss would come to talk to us. In the meantime, it started raining. I remember the rain lasted for three days. After about one hour, the same Suzuki 4X4 vehicle, three days. After about one hour, the same Suzuki 4X4 vehicle, as mentioned above, arrived to the spot with Aslan Luluni, Muharem Knushi, also known as Giqa, and Nimon Tofa's nephew, and one man whom I did not know but whom I later on recognised as Ramush Haradinaj." Now, first of all, is it right that Aslan Luluni came in the jeep?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, he came on foot with Nimon Tofa's nephew.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So did you tell the OTP investigator that he had come in the jeep?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, he came on foot. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then you describe what you say Aslan Luluni and Muharem Knushi and the fourth man were wearing. And then at paragraph 69, you're recorded as saying this: "The four of them were standing about two or three metres from where we were sitting." Is that right? Were they standing two or three metres from where you were sitting, or were they standing 20 or 30 metres, with bushes and trees in between, as you told us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a greater distance. Maybe I was wrong about the distance. It was a greater distance than two or three metres. If it had been just two or three metres, I would have been able to hear what they were saying, but it was a greater distance than two or three metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And as you've told us so far, it was that you couldn't hear what they were saying and the only word you could hear was "commandant"; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You go on, or are recorded as going on in this statement to say, "All of us could hear Aslan Luluni saying the following to the fourth man: 'Commander Ramush Haradinaj, the people we have captured are at your disposal.'" Now, yesterday I put that to you in terms and you said quite categorically you were sure you did not and could not have said anything like that. Did you or did you not hear one -- Aslan Luluni say, "Commander Ramush Haradinaj, the people we have captured are at your disposal." Did you hear it or did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. Just the word "commander."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So did the OTP investigator make this up for himself or was that something that you told him at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe it was an interpretation problem or maybe I said something, really. But it's such a long time ago that I can't recollect exactly how it was. Some things I did say. Not the whole sentence you just pronounced, but the word "commander," I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: This was read over to you in a language you understood, Witness 38, and you signed this page. Are you lying in the evidence that you're giving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I'm not lying. They did read it to me. That's right. But I'm really sorry, it's a long time ago. I really can't remember. But I gave statements in many places, as you can see for yourselves, but you must understand I was ill, I was in a state of shock. It was a great trauma to me. I heard the word "commander."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You weren't ill when you made this statement to the OTP investigator, were you, Witness 38?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I, who had never been -- had to worry in my life about sugar or fat in my blood, I suddenly have to watch out for all that and I have high blood pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And does that plain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, is there an audio recording of this interview? Does that exist?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Does your blood-sugar level explain why, in the first sentence of paragraph 70, you say that those words, "Commander Ramush Haradinaj, the people we have captured are at your disposal," that those words are how you and your relatives found out the identity of the man? Is that because of your blood sugar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know, I don't know. I'm really at the end of my wits. I'm really sorry. Maybe I did say that, but I was exhausted then. My sugar level was really high. But the truth is the only thing I heard then distinctly was "commander," and maybe I also heard --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not quite sure about the end of this sentence. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last part of your answer, where you said you heard the word "commander," and let me just see what -- "and maybe I also heard," you said. What did you maybe also heard -- hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only the word "commander." It was really 20 to 30 metres away from me and I couldn't. They were talking but I couldn't hear because I had been mistreated, slapped about, and I was sitting there by the mill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 38, I think Mr. Emmerson is trying to explore how to understand that a -- quite a couple years after this event took place you gave a statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, was Your Honour referring to this statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Seven and a half years after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That where you then told to the person who interviewed you that you knew about the name of Mr. Haradinaj because you then heard someone addressing him as "Commander Ramush Haradinaj," whereas in this courtroom you explained to us that you did not know the name at the time but that you recognised that person from television and that's how you found out that it was, as you said, Mr. Haradinaj. So in the statement you said: "It's because I heard others addressing him by his name and that's how I found out that it was Mr. Haradinaj," whereas in this courtroom you said: "It was because I saw him on television." Now, Mr. Emmerson is puzzled by these two quite different versions of how you found out about the identity of the person that appeared at the mill. Could you help him? Could you help us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll tell you all I know. I saw him there at the mill and I heard that man addressing him as commander, and then three or four months later I saw him on TV and I assumed that it must be the man because he had been addressed as commander. But at that time I was not quite certain that it was him, but when I saw him on TV I thought it was him and they addressed him as commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could we look at paragraph 73. I have two more paragraphs I need paragraphs I need to ask about before we can conclude. Could we look at paragraph 73. There you are recorded as having told the investigator that Ramush Haradinaj and Muharem Knushi ordered Aslan Luluni to search you and your father and to use force if necessary to get information from you. That's not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear what they said to me, but he returned. I didn't hear what was being said. But he returned and continued maltreating me, so that I assumed that had been the order given him.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: To search you when you were already naked.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had already been searched. I thought that he had been given the order to come and continue to maltreat us. That was my assumption. If someone comes and beats you up and goes and talks to a person and then returns and starts mistreating you again, that was what I just assumed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, would you please move to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Final question, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could we please look at 74, 75, and 76, because after this account that you have given, you then say: "Then," that is after those words you said were spoken, "Then Ramush Haradinaj was called over the radio. I could not hear what they were talking about, but I know that he and Knushi left the spot immediately. They left by the 4X4 Suzuki vehicle driven by Knushi. Aslan Luluni and Nimon Tofa's nephew stayed with us. Luluni first stripped my father naked in front of us." And then dropping down to paragraph 79: "When he finished beating my father, he turned to me. He stripped me naked as well and put a knife against my throat." Now, what you told the OTP investigator, Witness 38, is exactly what I suggest you told Mr. Di Fazio on Tuesday, which is that this incident of the jeep took place before you were abused and that at the time the jeep arrived, you had not been ill-treated, just as you said in the statement here and just as you told Mr. Di Fazio on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. They came before that and maltreated us, but in the meanwhile they stopped while they went to the jeep. And after that they returned to us again and maltreated us again for some 10 to 15 minutes and then they went away. But they brought a man to guard us and left him there with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 38, one of the questions that puzzles Mr. Emmerson at this moment is that at the time - at least that's how it's put on paper - that you were recorded to have said that you were stripped naked after the jeep had left, whereas your testimony in this court was that you were stripped naked already before the jeep arrived, that you were still naked when these people in the jeep were there. So there is a difference in these two versions of the story and Mr. Emmerson is puzzled by what's the right story and why is there a difference between these two versions. Do you have an explanation for that or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I know that before the jeep and after the jeep, they came and maltreated me, and I was stripped naked. Perhaps the questions asked me then were not the same -- were not phrased in the same way as you are putting them to me now, whether it was before or after, so I didn't give the proper question -- answer. But I was naked from the beginning to the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I've no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness 38, we'll have a break now. We'll resume at 4.30. Then there will be a relatively short examination by one of the other counsel, the Judges might have more questions for you, and we'll see whether there are any further questions to be put to you by the Prosecution. We stand adjourned until 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 38, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Guy-Smith is counsel for Mr. Balaj. Please proceed, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall being asked but a few moments ago concerning the weather conditions at the time that you were naked, as you have told us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You have told us that it had been raining heavily; it was very bad weather. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm -- I'm not connected, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you also have told us that it had rained for a period of some three days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand from the testimony that you've given here, you've indicated that at various times you were ill or sick, and it made it hard for you to remember things. But with regard to the issue of the rain, this is something that you have no doubt about, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, until the day when they drove us to Aslan Riza Djoci's house. It was raining until that day, and even that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My specific question to you is: When you were, as you've told us, naked for two days, was it raining continuously and heavily during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes it was raining heavily, sometimes less heavily, but it was constantly bad weather.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So if I understand your answer correctly, for purposes of the issue of the rain and the weather, there's no doubt in your mind that during that period of time, it was very bad weather and there was a great deal of rain; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mostly during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And it is, in fact, the combination of your nakedness, as you've told us, coupled with the rain, that is the reason that you had a bad fever; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was catching a cold.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that a review of meteorological records for that period of time establishes that there was no rain whatsoever, would your answer be any different?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I think "the period of time" should be specified to this witness so she can indicate -- stipulated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you consider to be the relevant period of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The relevant period of time is when she was -- when she claims to have been naked for two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you specify on what is covered by your information, your meteorological information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I can. That would be the 28th, the 29th, and the 30th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may put this specifically to the witness that for these days if -- for these days. Perhaps I could try to put it to the witness. Mr. Guy-Smith, Witness 38, has checked the meteorology for the 28th, 29th, and 30th of May, for 1998, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And he found in, well, let's say, the weather reports that there was no rain at that time in that area, and he asks whether you'd still -- whether your testimony still would be that it was raining and raining heavily at the time when the event took place, if you'd know about these weather reports.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, it was raining in the mountains heavily; then it would stop for a while; then it would start drizzling; then it started raining heavily again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I thank you for your assistance, Your Honour, and with the answer that the witness has given, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are you inclined to tender any weather reports? Or -- I mean, is that what you have on your mind or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am inclined to tender some weather reports. I can do it at this point in time or a later point in time or perhaps after discussion with the Prosecution, if we are able to agree to a fact, then we can do it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course. There are two issues, and that is the exact time frame and the content of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Indeed, so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
