utterances.text: If Your Honours please, if we get a weather report in two days' time or in three or four days' time, how can I re-examine on the matter? I don't know what's in this weather report. I've never seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, do you have a copy --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which sufficiently identifies, I take it, the region that's covered by the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That would be ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no objection against -- I mean, you would tender that then from the bar table. Another possibility would be to give it to Mr. Di Fazio and to give him an opportunity to see whether any agreement could be reached on it. If so, then of course the Chamber might be inclined to accept the agreement among the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm happy to do it either way, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think if you do it this way, and then if there's any follow-up that's needed, then the Chamber will hear from you. Witness 38, this is all procedure and I hope it doesn't bother you. Mr. Harvey, your position is still the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: It remains the same, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It remains the same. Then let's see whether the Judges have any questions. Yes. Judge Hoepfel has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to talk with you a little more about this car which was called a jeep, but then jeep is a trademark at the same time and then it was called a Suzuki, and it is a four-wheel drive, you said, or the papers said. Can you describe this car a little more detailed, and can you confirm that it was, or seen to be, the same car which you saw at two different occasions at two different places? Can you sum up a little more and -- once more, and give some details. What did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is the same vehicle that I used to see before, before the war. The same man was in the vehicle as before. It was a jeep; there was some lettering on the door or somewhere else, Suzuki. It was black. And I saw the same jeep during that incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What do you mean it's the same car, it's one and the same car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I had seen it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you as well. You described the -- what happened when you were at the mill. You described that your father had to undress but could put on his clothes again after that; that you were stripped naked and that you were, at least for some time, not allowed to put on your clothes again. Other persons in the group you were in, that is, your family members, among them other women as well, was one of them -- did any of them also have to take their clothes off or were you the only one, together with your father, who had to take your clothes off?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My sister-in-law and my step-mother were the only two other women, although there was another girl as well. I'm sorry. But I was the only one, together with my father, who was made to strip. He was allowed to put his clothes back on a little later but I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So none of the other women had to take her clothes off; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have a question of a totally different nature. You referred several times to KLA members, KLA. How would you identify someone as belonging to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, based on the fact that they were armed, although at that time some of them were in uniform, some in civilian clothes, in my opinion they couldn't have been anything else; they couldn't have been members of any other army but the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's go through it step by step. You say if someone was armed. Let's just assume no uniform but just carrying a weapon, would you consider that person to be a KLA member for that fact alone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as uniforms were concerned, how many armed men -- were they only men or were there also women armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see women, I saw men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many of these armed men were wearing uniforms, as opposed to being in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I don't know the exact number. I didn't see uniforms that often at the time. There was a very small number of men in uniform at the time. I can't tell you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would the same be true for armed men as well? Would you see most of the men armed not to be in uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say no, do you mean that not most of them were without uniforms, most of the armed men, or are you saying that most of them wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, most of them did not have uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even those who were armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if they were not wearing uniforms, what -- apart from carrying a weapon, was there any other feature that would assist you in concluding that these were KLA men or KLA members?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know the rules. Maybe there were other possibilities. I don't know what the rules were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about rules. But was there anything else, apart from that they were carrying a weapon, that you would say, Oh, that's a KLA person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't make any conclusions about that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that means, to say it in simple words, that if they would put away their weapons where they were not wearing uniforms, that if you couldn't see the weapon anymore that you could not identify them as KLA members? Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, those who were wearing uniforms, how could you -- were these specific uniforms for KLA? Were they different from any other uniforms you knew about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had similar uniforms to those of the Yugoslav People's Army, except that they had KLA insignia. They were similar in the sense that they were camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when you're talking about insignia, is that -- you identified during your testimony one emblem of the KLA. Were there more, or was that the only one, or ...?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe they were different shapes to those patches, but I think that KLA were written on all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And were these patches ever worn by someone who was not wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see those patches when I was up there. I mean among civilians, I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you say "civilians," but I was talking about men, armed, not in uniform, whether they -- whether you ever saw any of these patches on their clothing or their outfits.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. At that time, I didn't see any patches on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for these answers. Mr. Di Fazio, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just one or two matters, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just following on immediately from His Honour, the President's, questions, about men in uniforms and carrying weapons, when you were -- when you saw the convoy moving along, did any of the men in the convoy have weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, men in civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I just want to turn to an answer you gave to Mr. Emmerson earlier this afternoon. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's been five years and three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So she resides there at the -- she resided there for five years and three months, and do I understand your evidence to be that she continues to reside there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/38 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's all I have in re-examination, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like that -- to have that clarified before I give an opportunity. You earlier testified that you would see your sister-in-law once a month.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that was in Kosovo. I understood the question to mean the period before she was exiled from the village where she used to live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me check that, because it's my recollection, but I could look that up, that you were asked about where you resided now, whether she resided in that same country; that you then said, But we are at quite a distance; and that then the question was put to you how often you would see her. So that left the impression that it was in that country that you would see her once a month. Now you're saying that you saw her once a month before you left Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, it's that we are trying to find out precisely what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem. Mr. Emmerson, is there any need for further questions? Mr. Guy-Smith? Mr. Harvey?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Witness 38, this concludes your testimony. We have asked many questions to you; you've answered the questions of the parties, of the Bench. We'd like to thank you for coming to The Hague and giving testimony before this court. You'll be escorted out of the courtroom by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, for hearing me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would first like to -- yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Before we proceed to the next witness, I left a message earlier on simply to say that there are rather a number of matters that need to be resolved for next week, and I didn't want the situation to arise in which we broke at ten to 7.00 and found that there was insufficient time to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So I suggested perhaps this would be the right moment. But in addition to that, I think we need to revisit the question that I agreed to leave over during my cross-examination arising from Mr. Di Fazio's proofing notes and the question that I put to the witness. Can I remind Your Honours, unless -- if this is a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's a convenient moment. We have a few procedural matters, and perhaps we'll deal with them at this moment before the Prosecution calls its next witness. But if you would not mind, Mr. Emmerson, that I first ask another question which is also still pending; that is, in what way will the Chamber receive a response to the last request for protective measures filed by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think the response will be in writing and I think Mr. Guy-Smith will outline his position, which we will adopt, since these witnesses primarily are witnesses that he'll be cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when could we expect?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Guy-Smith, you're tasked by Mr. Emmerson with providing a written response to the motion for protective measures. We'd like to know when you intend to file that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It will be filed by Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By Monday. And, Mr. Re, I don't think that that causes any problems as far as, I don't know, arrival. I should have to look up exactly which witnesses these are and whether they're scheduled for anywhere where we could expect for them to arrive already before Monday in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I be reminded of which -- the witness numbers. It would certainly assist me. A lot of filings here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wasn't it 9 and 15, or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think it's 4 and 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 4 and 19, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No problem at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Causes no problems. Okay. Then, Mr. Guy-Smith, we're looking forward to your response to be filed Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think also you'd been searching for something in the transcript, Your Honour. I'm not sure with regard to whether Witness 38 and the sister-in-law lived in the same country, and whether -- when they saw each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since the witness has left the courtroom, I don't think whether there's -- whether there's any point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We just found it for you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. I just search and then -- the name of the country and then you get it very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't know where we're turning to next, but two issues did arise during our prior session; one was the issue of proofing and the other was the issue of audio recordings, where you specifically asked about audio recordings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, whether they existed or not. I take it, Mr. Emmerson, that that's the same issue you'd like to address, or at least one of the issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think it might be helpful if I directed Your Honours' attention to the transcript at page 14, line 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Of today?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Of today, yes, this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Where arising out of the questions that have been asked on the proofing notes, and in particular the sentence which reads -- which states that until that time, in effect, there had been no ill-treatment. I sought clarification from Witness 38 by asking her the direct question: "Did you or did you not tell Mr. Di Fazio on Tuesday that, by the time the jeep arrived, you had already been stripped naked and assaulted? Did you tell him that or did you not?" And she replied: "I think I did, yes." Now, we obviously need to have Mr. Di Fazio to respond that and to say whether that was said to him or it was not. Now, I'm anxious as to what the implications of that are, but there can be no question, in our submission, but that he must be called upon to state whether that was, in fact, said to him or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have two questions, the first one being that Mr. Di Fazio can express himself on whether he thinks that this is what could reasonably be expected from him, and only if that question is answered in the positive, then of course the next question would be whether or not the witness told him this during proofing sessions -- during the proofing session. Mr. Di Fazio, so I split up the questions clearly in two, the first one of a procedural nature. Mr. Re, if you would like to answer that question, no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's probably better that I answer this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio won't be giving evidence in this court as to what was said. There was an interpreter there who interpreted whatever the witness said to Mr. Di Fazio. If ever the need arose to clarify what was said by the witness and then what was translated to Mr. Di Fazio, the interpreter would be the appropriate person to provide the necessary declaration or affidavit of what was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, with the advantage that the interpreter can not only provide an answer to the question what the witness told to the interpreter, but also to what the interpreter told to Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry, but if this matter is to be properly investigated, there is the possibility that the interpreter's recollection will differ from Mr. Di Fazio's, who was writing it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And so I'm afraid that doesn't represent quite such a neat solution to the issue of the position that Mr. Di Fazio is in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're one step in front of --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're saying "if" there's a difference. We do not know yet. The Chamber will consider it all, I think, and we might need a bit more time for that, to see -- we'd like to think it over.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd -- if you would want to make further submissions on the matter, then perhaps, very briefly, in ten or twelve lines, if you just say there has to be an investigation, that's all --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: All I was going to say is, we won't know if there is a difference of recollection if the Prosecution takes the position that Mr. Di Fazio is not called upon to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider the matter. It's not at this moment an urgent moment, I think, because the witness has been excused. Several things go through my mind. I'd like to check whether the same things go through the minds of my colleagues. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would like to add what I think is a systemic concern. I wrote a letter to the Prosecutor on the 19th of January specifically dealing with the issue of proofing. I will be more than happy to supply that letter to the Chamber at a later point today, but I will read you two paragraphs of that letter so you can see that the precise problem that I forecast has now come up. "Finally, I suggest that to ensure a full, complete, and accurate record of the 'proofing sessions' --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you? Is that a letter from late January that has just been filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's a letter of January 19th in which we suggested -- we suggested a full and complete record, either audio, video, or, if nothing else, stenographic recordings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think we have a comprehensive response to that letter from the Prosecution. Mr. Re, the Chamber will consider whether it will invite you to give a response to that, perhaps also in light of the experience we have now. But before the Chamber invites you, I will try to find out whether there is a sufficient majority in the Chamber to invite you. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We did respond to the letter. If there's any question about that, we responded to the letter. I doubt it was copied to the Trial Chamber. I wouldn't see any reason to copy it to the Trial Chamber. There's a lot of letters that go between Defence and Prosecution that aren't copied to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But this one was specifically brought to the attention of the Trial Chamber. If there's a response, I think it would be good for the Trial Chamber to know that response. We will then first read it and see whether any further action is needed. Yes? Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might. You had also asked another question which was a question with regard to the issue of audio recordings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe the Chamber probably has another letter that I wrote. There were two letters, I wrote, I think, in that regard. One was on the 10th of letter; the other was on the 18th. We have received a response from the Prosecution in that regard indicating all of the audio recordings that exist and all of the video recordings that exist. I'm more than happy to supply a copy of that letter to the Chamber so that when the issue comes up again, which I'm sure that it will since, for example, the video recording that we discussed -- that was discussed today was not contained in that letter, the Chamber will be aware of at least what information we have at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the Chamber might not be that interested in reviewing long lists of what is recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sure the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Sure. The Chamber would like, if any issue arises which might be resolved by recording, to be immediately informed about whether a recording exists, yes or no, because if no recording exists, we don't have to even try to seek a solution in that direction; if it does exist, then we could consider that. Yes. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only remaining matter is if there's any update on the order of calling witnesses next week. Earlier we heard about problems. What could we reasonably expect and what still bothers the Defence as far as these witnesses are concerned in terms of disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's one witness in particular, and I've been mentioning him from time to time over the last few days. There's no difficulty, I think, with mentioning his name in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's always keep on the safe side. I mean, it could be -- if the Prosecution says under no circumstances there are protective measures, then please go ahead; if not, then please refer to him on the list, and I've got all the lists available here.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: He is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under filed list, chronological order, if you could ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think on the filed list, so long as Your Honour and I are looking at the same version, he should be Witness 8, witness number 82.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 8 is on my list; 82, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So this witness is a former employee of the Serbian State Security Service, and he's made two witness statements in this case; one in May 2003 and one in April 2006. In addition, the Defence were provided earlier this week with some proofing notes dated Thursday, the 1st of March, a reference of videolink proofing session. Now, just to sketch in the background very briefly. He purports to give general evidence, drawing conclusions about the operation of the KLA in the Dukagjin region over a considerable period of time. None of his statements are sourced within the witness statements, so there is no indication of the particular source that he is drawing on. He simply gives a general indication that the State Security Service had available to it a combination of intercept material, human intelligence reports, that type of general information. There was very little in the form -- in the form of clarification of the issues that Your Honours identified as issues that would require to be explored in cross-examination when secondary testimony, which is what this is, is -- it comes to be given. So the Defence is in the position, to start with, that we can't tell from the witness statement what the sources of the material or the statements might be. That's the first point. You may remember that earlier, I think perhaps last Thursday at the Pre-Trial Conference, I mentioned the fact that Mr. Re had told me that from Belgrade a batch of material had just been received, and that we understood that it might be particularly relevant to one of the early witnesses and that Mr. Re identified Witness 8 as the witness to whom that material was potentially relevant. In his first witness -- I'm sorry, in his second witness statement, he is effectively asked for source material and says that the source material could be provided by the Serbian State Security Service. He also refers, I think in his first statement, to some 64 files of material which have been provided to the Prosecution on which he could comment, if asked. It's not clearly whether that 64 volumes of material or the material that was supposed to be in the Belgrade selection contains material that could properly be his source material. We were told two days ago that the proofing note we have is incomplete in the sense that there was to be a further proofing session. I don't know whether the position has changed in that regard. But this proofing note concludes - and this is a less significant problem than the ones I've averted to - but just before I drew the inference together, this statement concludes with a passage that says, "Mr. --" the witness was given and read over a number of VJ reports and was asked in general whether he could comment on them. He said he was familiar with the contents of the reports and could comment on them. There's then listed eight reports and their ERN numbers. There are no comments, so we don't know what comments he might be proposing to make. Now, I asked Mr. Re some time ago and he indicated that he would kindly oblige, just to identify, first of all, what it is from this witness it's proposed to elicit so that we can begin to look at what the source material might be, so that we can prepare cross-examination on the lines that Your Honour has indicated ought to be pursued; and secondly, to identify what, if any, exhibits the witness was proposing to produce, whether they came from either of those two batches of material or not. And it had been my intention to suggest that we proceed in stages. That the Prosecution do that, identify the exhibits they might wish the witness to produce, and that the Defence can then consider what further disclosure would be required, because one of the problems is that if either of those two batches of material contain source documents that the Defence could properly use to challenge the factual expressions that the witness proposes to give, then we need to have an opportunity to see the material, to examine it, and to prepare cross-examination. But at the moment, as matters currently stand, this witness is document-light. We have had no disclosure of source material at all other than a proofing note which lists eight VJ reports, which are obviously not his concern because he's State Security, not VJ, and on which we've been told he can comment but not told what his comments are. Now, my suggestion to Mr. Re has been that he's not ready to call this witness, but I don't, as I've emphasised from the outset, want to be put in the position again and again where I have to be making applications for adjournments because the Prosecution hasn't put us in a position where the witness can properly and fairly be examined. So that is the situation that we're in. As far as the other witnesses are concerned, we're in the position to deal with any witness that the Prosecution has so far indicated it is able to call next week, other than this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, the issue is that Defence is uncertain about what you want to elicit from these witnesses; that it is uncertain about what additional material it could expect; that where eight reports have been identified as reports on which the witness will comment, that they do not know what the comment is. Could you help us out or could you help the Defence out?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We are, as I speak here in court, speaking to that witness by videolink to finish, to finalise, the proofing of him. I would anticipate that that would be finished within the next couple of hours and we will have the information to the Defence later tonight or tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would, most likely, these proofing notes give an answer to at least some or -- if not all, of the questions raised by Mr. Emmerson, I mean about what you're seeking to elicit from him, what material is there to be commented on, what his comments are on this material?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, if the proofing's finished, it certainly will, because the documents we intend to show to the witness we would have shown to him by videolink as I speak now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There are six documents referred to in the proofing notes furnished earlier this week. They're VJ documents; they're all on the exhibit list. Our intention at the moment, as far as I know, is only to show the witness documents which are on the exhibit list, and only ask him to comment on documents which are on the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many would that, approximately, be? Because I do understand that he was considered to be, a new word for me, a "document-light" witness. I mean, would the six or eight, difference of two only, would that expound to 60 or to 22 or -- I mean, could you give us an expression -- an impression on how document-light or how document-heavy you would finally be?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I would be guessing if I gave you a number. My Lotus Notes just crashed when I was trying to find it in a document I had. If I said around 30, it's a guess. Now, Mr. Emmerson referred to some 64 binders. Yes, the witness did refer to the fact that 64 binders of material might well have been provided to the OTP by Serbian intelligence at one point, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You consider that not relevant material for this witness. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, absolutely. Of course we're not going to ask him for 64 binders of material to be produced, or even look at them, in court. I think Mr. Emmerson's concern is he wants to see the 64 binders which are mentioned in the -- in the letter. Now, clearly there is some -- the Prosecution's disclosure obligations go only so far, and so far as I'm concerned, we've complied with that disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you don't use them, of course, this disclosure regime for documents to be tendered and produced into evidence, of course, is different from other documents. But, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's some help in the sense that Mr. Re has indicated that this witness will produce and comment on 30 documents. Now, my expectation is that these will be documents of some technical character.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I didn't say 30, I said I would be guessing if I said 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's -- gentlemen, gentlemen. If a reference is made to 30, everyone has understood that Mr. Re did not say anything as -- not 29 or 31. Let's try to understand each other in a way --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But not six or eight. And they will be documents of some technical character because of the nature of the witness's evidence. So the first question is, and I'm not purporting to answer it at this present stage but I am purporting, and have for some time been trying to give early-warning signals. The first problem is, if you have 30 documents of a technical character in terms of military and intelligence material, that material will need to be assimilated, assessed, and compared with other material before it can properly be the subject of cross-examination. So that's the first problem, however many documents it is. We also have had a history, as you know, of having material that -- on the Prosecution exhibit list for which no translations have been provided. But, again, until we know what these documents are. But the biggest question in this, if I may say so, is what I didn't hear from Mr. Re is that this witness' testimony will be confined to giving and commenting on those documents, because in his witness statements, the witness makes statements about what their position was. Now for the Defence to be able to explore the questions that Your Honour has identified, particularly the source of the statement and the reliability of the source, we need to know what the source of the statements that they are proposing to elicit from this witness are and have the material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I suggest we do the following. You've expressed your concerns. I'm afraid we can't resolve them right away. You'll receive within a couple of hours the new -- the new proofing notes which at least give an answer to, if not all, then at least some questions put to you. Then I also noticed that from now on, just looking at this order, but I don't have the exact order in my mind, that at least a couple of other witnesses will first be called before this witness will be called, or is he the first one for next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, he's the first one for Monday. The difficulty we have is that the second one has now -- who was our anticipated second one, we've just filed another application before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time -- well, if that's for Monday. We can't speculate on what you'll find in your letter-box this evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I just didn't want to turn up on Monday and make an application that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. If there's -- I would like the parties to try to resolve the matters once they have received -- once they have received the newest proofing notes and what exhibits and what comments, et cetera; then to see to what extent they can resolve the issues. And therefore, Mr. Re, if you provide the material late Friday evening, I'm afraid that I have to condemn you to be available also during the weekend, unless very exceptional circumstances would prevent you from being addressed. I mean, Monday is Monday. I mean, that's only the weekend in between. And in return, if this would create major problems, we'll put a system in place that the Chamber can be approached during the weekend as well to -- at least to report to the Chamber what the problems are.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I should make it clear. I wouldn't have been troubling you with this issue at all had it not been for the fact that the Prosecution were proposing to call the witness on Monday. Had it been later in the week, I wouldn't have been bothering you with this at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So the parties will informed -- first of all, I invite you to try to resolve any matters, but, of course, we're now more or less speculating because you do not know what to expect in the proofing notes; we do not know how much material it is; we do not know how technical the material is. We just don't know. So first try to find out what we're really talking about; then try to resolve it. If there's any problem; if not, then the Chamber might be in a position to assist you, if it were only from a distance. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Two brief things. One is not only do we not know the nature of the information contained in the documents, but we obviously do not know the length of the documents submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the second thing is, and I guess I'm starting to hear myself in my own head a fair amount, which is I heard the words "This particular individual is being proofed by videolink," and I would request that the Chamber order - and he is being proofed as we speak right now - that the Chamber order that the videolink be recorded so in the event there are any difficulties in the future, there is something that can be done in that regard. Obviously, it would stay within the possession of the Prosecution at this time. So we don't run into the problem and we have a safeguard for the problem we ran into today, it seems to be a very easy solution to something that otherwise could potentially come up again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. Of course, you would not ever expect this Chamber to give any order on something that is technically not possible, and I just do not know at this moment. So my first question to Mr. Re would be: Is there any technical possibility of recording such a videolink, I mean technical possibility to be put in place quickly? I mean, are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd have to make relevant inquiries of the technical people to find out if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's do that for the future. I also understand at the same time, that the proofing notes -- proofing will be finalised in a couple of hours. So, therefore, to say now the last two hours we have to buy new equipment, I mean, it's a matter which certainly should be on the agenda for the future. A general question, that is, to what extent will the Prosecution be required to record and provide recordings, and what kind of recordings, et cetera, that is a question which we'll have to deal with rather quickly, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber does not issue an order at this moment for the remainder of this -- of this proofing, through videolink, of this witness, but it is on our agenda. If that's everything for the time being, then we'd like to invite the Prosecution to call its next witness. But before doing so, I'd like to go into private session. Mr. Harvey, I've forgotten you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, merely this: If the Court would be so kind as to excuse me from the remainder of this session, Mr. Troop will, of course, remain here and my client consents to my absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for informing us, Mr. Harvey. Before the next witness will be called, I'd like to go -- I have two matters. I'd like to deal with the exhibits of the previous witness. Both parties have presented documents that were marked for identification. Does the -- any of the Defence object to any of the documents tendered by the Prosecution? And the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, yes, I don't think the meteorological report should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's not tendered. The solution found was that Mr. Guy-Smith will speak with you, and only after that but then from the bar table, as I understand, tender the document -- if there's any need --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. In the light of that, of course, I'll speak to my learned colleague and we'll, I'm sure, settle the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour is asking, obviously, about the exhibits tendered during the course of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, not anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The first witness, we have not dealt finally about those, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are waiting for a final submission by the Prosecution of the documents in the right chronological order, and we'll refrain from any decision until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So, so far as this witness is concerned, there's no issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Then, Madam Registrar, perhaps you could tell us what numbers - I could look it up in the e-court as well - but that starts from P -- is it, 7 or 8? The documents marked for identification and tendered during the testimony of this witness. [Trial Chamber and registrar confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The exhibits marked for identification -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The exhibits marked for identification until now, P7, P8, P9, and D2, D3, and D4 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think, unless it's been corrected ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All of them under seal. But, Mr. Emmerson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't check myself. I should correct myself and add D1 to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, there are two other problems, apparently, on the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: First of all, D2 is marked P2, so that needs to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And secondly, D3 is exhibited as the translation, and I think the practice is that the English translation should be exhibited -- the English original should be exhibited but the translation linked to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Otherwise, those are the four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for this adjustment. But they are admitted into evidence, with the correction just stated. Then, Mr. Re, I'm wondering what's the best way to proceed. We need another break. Perhaps it would be better that we have the break now and then you can call the witness. Isn't that the best solution? We'll then have a break of 20 minutes. We'll resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just a very brief update. We've had some discussion between the parties, and -- and one witness who is due to be called on Tuesday at the moment, who is witness number 5, is due to travel to The Hague on Monday, arriving at 11.30. He is a witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At night or in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In the morning. He's a witness of fact. We could very easily be ready to deal with him in the afternoon. And so if the problems which I foresee in relation to the witness we were discussing before the break materialise, that is a witness who, in theory, could be substituted. Now, I think Mr. Re has indicated that until he does arrive, it won't be clear whether he needs a rest between arrival and testifying, and I absolutely understand that, although of course one possibility might be to sit just a little later --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that seems to be an escape for the situation, at least to use our time --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- we'd like to be informed what the final solution will be. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We do, of course, understand the point being made by the Defence. I have no objection, in principle, to calling that witness before -- before the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But it may mean that it's a bit difficult to bring him straight from the plane and put him in the witness box.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's understood. We only say that's a possible escape if the other problem would materialise. That's good to know. I'd like to go into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Re, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I am. It will be Witness 58.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes -- no, I made a mistake, as a matter of fact. We have to go back into private session for another moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Is there -- for face distortion, we always have to be careful that the entrance of the witness is not shown on the screen, and at a later stage, we'll, in public, deliver the decision granting the protective measures because that has to be done in public and cannot be done in private session only. Are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I do understand that that is a witness testifying under pseudonym, that is, Witness 58.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will obviously briefly need to go into private session at the beginning of her testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Not yet. First, I think. I take it that you'll first deal with the pseudonym sheet and then go into private session for her personal background.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't have a pseudonym sheet as such. There's no point in me showing her a pseudonym sheet. I can prepare one afterwards for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you make a piece of paper with the name and without any further explanation, just the date of birth on it, then -- because we cannot accept that there's a witness testifying in this court who has not confirmed her identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is there any reason why I can't ask her in private session what her name is and put that in private session on the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's another way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Good afternoon. Witness 58, I'm talking -- I'm talking to you. Witness 58, we'll not call you by your name. We have decided that, for various reasons, it's better that we'll call you Witness 58.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. Would you please -- may I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My question, first of all, is: Can you read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would like to seek the assistance of a ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Here we need the assistance of the translators. If you would -- I will give the solemn declaration in English. Would you please translate that to the witness, and then we'll ask the witness to repeat that. So I will first say it in English --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you'll hear it in your earphones in your language, and then I'd like you to repeat that solemn declaration. The declaration is: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Would you please say this in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 58, you'll first be examined by Mr. Re, who is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Re, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can we just go into private session for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Witness, where were you living in 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Myself? You mean when I was a girl or when I was married?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In 1998, that's when the fighting was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: I was in Ponoshevc.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What's Ponosevac? Is it a town, a village, a city?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: No, it's not a city, it's a village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who were you living there with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: With my sister-in-law, with my brother -- sorry, with my father-in-law and with my kids, with my husband's family.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. How many children do you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Two girls.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were they living with you in 1998 in Ponosevac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: No. Before yes, but not at the war-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Are you a Roma person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did your family leave Ponosevac in 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: My family doesn't live in Ponosevac, it lives in Junik.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You said you were living there in 1998.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How did you come to leave Ponosevac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Because they came and told us to leave, both the Albanians and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Which Albanians came and told you to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: I don't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How do you know that you had to leave because Albanians came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: They came -- first it was the Serbs who came to our house. You could tell the Albanians from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What did the Serbs do when they came to your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: They said, You have to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you there then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: I was there with my father-in-law and with my kids, in Ponoshevc.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: It was nine years ago, on the 5th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did the Albanians come before or after the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: First came the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you go back to your home after the Serbs had told you, you had to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: No. I stayed for two days, and then when the Albanians came and told me to leave, I left for Junik.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Why did the Serbs tell you and your family you had to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: They said, You have to leave because you cannot stay here anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you given a reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: They said, You have to leave, all of you. You must not stay here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who is "all of you"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: We could tell them. Some spoke Serbian, some didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Who is the "all of you" who were told to leave? Is it your family or some other people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: No. It was only us; I, with my children and my father-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You said the Albanians came a little while later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Tell the Court, tell the Judges, about what happened when the Albanians came. Firstly, were you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Yes. I was at home. I was at home. But I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Are you talking about Ponosevac or somewhere else, when you said the Albanians came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Are you asking me about Ponosevac?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Or about Junik?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm asking you about Ponosevac.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I told you. Then we left and then I went to Junik, to stay with my sister-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Why did you leave -- why did you leave Ponosevac? What did the Albanians say to you about why you had to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: They said to us that, You are with the Serbs. Your sister-in-law is working with the Serbs. Then we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who were these Albanians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: I said I don't know them. I didn't know them. They had balaclavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Where did you go when you left Ponosevac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: We went to Junik, to my sister-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Why did you go to Junik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Because I was scared. I took my children and my father-in-law, and I went to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: But they fired there, too. I stayed there, I don't remember, I think two or three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. What sort of residence did your sister-in-law have in Junik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: It was not hers. It was given to her by the state, by the government, because of her work. It was an old house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You just said you stayed in Junik for two or three weeks. What happened after two or three weeks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: They came and fired at the apartment. We were having a coffee in the morning; it was 8.00. And a bullet also hit one of the walls, even in the room where we were, and they broke the glass. And then they came and told us that, You have to leave, and we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who were the people who came to the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: I didn't know them. They just told us to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What sort of people were they, men or women, for example?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: No, no, they were all men, and they were many numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: KLA clothes. We could tell that they were members of KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What was it about what they were wearing that -- how could you tell they were KLA members?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: They had that red -- red badge, I don't know, like a flag, on the arm, on the arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness be displayed in e-court 65 ter exhibit 1173.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And may I, meanwhile, ask in what language they spoke to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They spoke Albanian. Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And this is also your own mother tongue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you repeat it, please? I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What is your own mother tongue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mother? No, I speak Albanian. I speak a little Roma.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: A moment ago you said the men who came to the house were wearing red badges. Just have a look at the document which is on the screen in front of you. What can you tell the Court about that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: I don't know, it's KLA, the sign of the KLA. You could tell that they were KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: By that, are you saying they were wearing badges looking like the one on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know what to tell you. You could tell that they were KLA. I told them they had yellow clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just have a look at the red badge on the screen in front of you. What can you say about that red badge compared to the red badges you said they were wearing, the men who came to your house? Is it the same badge or a different badge, or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: No, I -- I didn't know them. There were many of them. I told you that there were many.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm only asking you about -- I'm just asking you about the badge at the moment. What can you say about the badge on the screen? Same badge, different badge, or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: This is different from the one I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How different is it? What are the differences?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: This has this KLA, and the Serbs had another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand what you just said; the Serbs had one, the KLA had one. I'm talking about the badges the men who came to the house in Ponosevac were wearing. You said they were KLA people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes, they were of the KLA, but there were also Serbs. I explained to you before. What can I tell you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it was my -- I apologise. I meant Junik, not Ponosevac. I apologise. When they came to the house in --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: You are talking about Junik or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm talking about Junik. Look at that badge there. Is that the same badge or a different badge, or you don't know, that the men who came to the house were wearing when they came to Junik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: No, another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. What was the difference? What was the difference between this badge and the badge the KLA men who came to the house in Junik were wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: What can I tell you now? The Serbs had, like, yellow, black --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's explanation: By "yellow," sometimes they refer to green, sometimes to blue. So she's saying yellow but maybe you have to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you describe what the badge looked like that the KLA members were wearing when they came to the house in Junik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: I couldn't recognise them. They were wearing masks. I told them that day, too, that I didn't know them, didn't recognise them. They were many.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What can you tell us about the badge they were wearing? I'm only talking about the badge.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: You can see the sign here on the screen. There is no other sign. You can see that this is the sign of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Maybe I'm confusing you. Is that the same badge that they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: What can I tell you? I'm not an educated person. I don't know what to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Does it look like it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, has this document a number already? It very much looks like P9, which is now Exhibit P9, meanwhile, but you didn't refer to it as such. Mr. Re, I have the paper copy which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The suggestion raised by the Registry is that the document which we find now on our screen and which was earlier not on our screen but seems to reflect similar but a bit distorted, bad colours, that P9 is replaced by the document with the ERN number U0158334, because it seems to depict exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's entirely correct. I'm informed they have been -- 116 -- sorry, 1173 is a clearer and cleaner and better picture of P9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then P9 will be replaced by the better version of what is the same document or the same picture, as a matter of fact. Please proceed, Mr. Re. And that's, then, P9, the new P9, which is shown to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Before we talked about the badge a few minutes ago, you said, "They came and fired at the apartment" at 8.00 in the morning. They came into the room and said, "You have to leave and we left."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What did they do when they came in the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What did they do when they came in the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Excuse me. They said -- may I just have some water, please. They said, You have to leave here. They said to my sister-in-law, You have killed people and you have to leave from here. And I have told you during the previous time we met that they told us that we have to leave from there, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. When you said, "I have told you during the previous time," you're referring to me or to someone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: I'm referring to those who told us that we had to leave. They said, You have to leave under no other condition. You have killed people. We were crying. And my sister-in-law said to them that, I don't -- I haven't killed anyone, but they told her that, You have to leave from here anyways.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who was with you, apart from your sister-in-law, when you were in the house and the shots were fired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: My sister-in-law, both sister-in-laws, my father-in-law's wife, myself, and the two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the sister-in-law you're referring to, is that -- is that the sister-in-law number 38?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What did you all do when they told you to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: We took to the road and they told us that we have to go take the road to Gacifer, because Gacifer is not very far, two or three minutes away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who is "they" who told you, you had to take that road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Those Albanians who also went out with their families, with their children, and the KLA members. We went out and we were sent to a house. It was -- it resembled a basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just going back one moment, was it the KLA members who told you, you had to take the road or someone else who told you, you had to take the road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: These were others. There were KLA members and there were others who were not with uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How far away was this house that resembled a basement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Not very far. Maybe about 20 minutes away. I don't remember exactly, but it wasn't very far from the house of my sister-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you -- did any of you have any possessions with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did any of you have any things with you, apart from people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Yes. The second sister-in-law had a bag with her. There were some clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How many in total were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Well, as I said earlier, I was with my father-in-law, with my sister-in-law, with children, myself. There were others as well. There were many Albanians. There was a person called Jusuf Syla and his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What did you do when you got to this house, the one that resembled a basement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Well, what did we do? We stayed there. Then some others came and they said, You have to leave this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who were the others who came there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: I didn't know them. There were a lot. It was war. I was concerned about my children. I was looking after them. They were small. They were afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Why did you go to this particular place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Nimon Tofa took us out. He said, You have to go there, and don't be afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Why this particular place and not any other one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Well, the children were crying and he said that, You have to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The ones who came, the others who came there and told you, you had to leave, were they -- what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: They were civilians, in civilian clothes, and two or three of them, I don't know exactly, I think were KLA members. And as I already explained, my children were small. I wasn't feeling very well. It was cold, it was raining, and we didn't have jackets. I was completely lost. I was looking after my children. I was ill myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Whereabouts in this house were you -- did you go when you went there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: You mean after we left Gaciferi, that place?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Well, after that we left, after they told us we had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, no, no. After you left your sister-in-law's house in Junik and you went to this other place that resembled a basement, whereabouts in that place did you go to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: To Gacifer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Gacifer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Whereabouts in the house? Whereabouts in the house were you sheltering?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: When I left my sister-in-law's place, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Then they took us and they said that, You have to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yeah, I know. I'm asking you: You went to this house. Whereabouts in the house did you go to, top floor, bottom floor? Where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: It was in the bottom part, in the basement. It was a basement. I don't know whose house it was. It was somebody else's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the people who came into the house and told you, you had to go, what did they say to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: They said, You have to leave from here because you have killed three persons, and she said, We haven't killed anyone. We were looking after our children. And they told her that she had killed some people in the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you remember if those people had any weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What sort of weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Well, excuse me, I apologise, but I didn't pay attention to the weapons. I was looking after my children. I was scared and we didn't dare look much. I don't know what kind of weapons they had. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you remember whether they were big weapons or small weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Big ones. I know they were big weapons, but what kind, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, could you just seek to clarify this, because "big weapons" could mean a lot of things compared to smaller weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you know what a rifle is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Well, how shall I explain this? I don't know what a rifle is. I didn't pay attention. They had weapons, but as to what kind of weapons, whether they were big or small, I didn't pay attention, I didn't see. But they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you remember how they were -- I withdraw that. Were they carrying the weapons or were the weapons somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: I don't know, but they had some in their hands. They had one weapon in their hands, but I can't remember everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you know the difference between a pistol and a rifle, a pistol being a small one and a rifle being a long one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Well, something like this. Neither big, nor small. Some were small, some were big. They had weapons. They had both big weapons and small weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The witness was indicating hands held apart about 30 centimetres apart, for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would rather say anything between 70 and 90, 30 centimetres being this. This is what is my recollection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know, and I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What did you do when they told you to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: We then went to Tofaj. I took my children and we all went to Tofaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How far is Tofaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Well, maybe 20 or 30 minutes away. I really don't remember. It was crowded. The children were crying.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: But I would say about 20, 25 minutes away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Where did you go in Tofa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: At the mill. We stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is that in the countryside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Tofaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Is that in the countryside or the town itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: No, no, it wasn't a town. Erenik was there. There was water there, there was mountain there, there was a mill there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Why did you go there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Why? Because we were scared. We were scared because even in Gacifer they said that we had to leave, and we went there thinking that we might be safe. There were a lot of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the people who -- who you were with when you went towards Tofaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: You mean from the Albanians? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You said there were a lot of people when you went to Tofaj. What were they, Serb, Albanian, Roma, or what were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: No, no, Albanians. All of them were Albanians and only us were Romas, the family of my husband and myself. The others were all Albanians with their families and children. There were a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You said you saw some KLA members in Junik. Did you see any KLA people at the mill?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: You mean at the mill? Yes. Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What were they wearing and what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: There were many, but -- they had yellow KLA clothes. You could tell them. You could tell who the members of the KLA were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You just said they were wearing yellow. I just want to clarify something.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: I know that they were yellow, but, as I said earlier, I wasn't paying much attention, I wasn't looking around. Those that I saw, I know that they had yellow clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I just want to show you a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could you please show the witness this piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just have a look of the piece of paper I'm showing you and tell me what colour it is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: It is yellow. To me it's yellow. Yellow clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the record reflect that I've shown the witness what I think in English would be described as a green piece of paper, but I understand that there's an Albanian yellow/green word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems to be a light shade of green, but yes, it's on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were these KLA members armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Yes, they were. There were a lot. I didn't know them. I couldn't recognise them. As I said earlier, I didn't know them. But there were a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How did they react to your group? What did they do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Well, a certain Aslan, whom I knew, came and he maltreated us a lot, my sister-in-law and father-in-law. And I went behind the mill and I was there for some 20 minutes, because the children were crying, together with the wife of my father-in-law, because they had taken the bag from my second sister-in-law. They wanted to search it. They turned it upside down. And then I said, Please do not do this to us. And he said, Oh, you should be killed. This person I knew. Then I took the second sister-in-law, because they wanted to rape her, and the children, and together with the wife of my father-in-law, we went away from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. I just ask you to pause there for a moment. Describe this person Aslan to the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/58
utterances.text: Aslan, him I know. He came there at the mill and he lined us up and he said, You should be killed because you are with the Serbs. He said this to the elder sister-in-law. He told her, You work with the Serbs and you should be killed. And then I took the second sister-in-law, since I cannot mention her name, and then he took this bag and I begged him not to take anything from there. There were some clothes, minor things. He turned everything upside down, put everything outside the bag on the ground. And I begged him, Don't do this to us, Aslan. Then, together with the sister-in-law and the children, I left from there, while the elderly sister-in-law and the father-in-law, they experienced these kinds of problems, whereas I, with the children and with the second sister-in-law, left that site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I'm looking at the clock. We might need one or two minutes for other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 58, it's 7.00. That's the time when we finish. We'd like you to come back on Monday, in the afternoon, quarter past 2.00. And I want to instruct you not to speak with anyone, whether you know someone well or whether you do not know someone, not to speak about the testimony you have given until now and also not about the testimony still to be given. So you should not speak with anyone at this moment about this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, just a moment. We are done for today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are done for today, but we'd like you to come back after the weekend, Monday, quarter past 2.00. The Victims and Witnesses Unit will take care of you so that you find your way and that's -- yes? Then, Madam Usher will now escort you out of the courtroom. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I may have missed it. I'm sorry, I did miss it. I've just seen it on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just want to inform the parties, if there's any need to get in touch with the Chamber staff, I take it that you have the communication details. You would have to call Mr. Zahar on his mobile phone. Mr. Zahar knows how to reach me, if need be. That's one. Then another matter. Mr. Re, I do understand that it's not easy to examine a witness like this witness. Nevertheless it would have, for example, saved time that when you asked her to describe Aslan, and then you let her go for ten lines, at least, to repeat what she said already, and nothing in it described Mr. Aslan. It's just a matter of a gentle interruption, and since -- would have done. And since I cannot exclude that similar things might happen in the future, I just give you this guidance. If there's no other procedural matter at this moment, we'll adjourn until Monday, the 12th of March, quarter past 2.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 12th day of March, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
